claims.text: The investigated material is a quaternary equiatomic FCC solid-solution alloy.
The alloy has a chemically disordered lattice and high configurational entropy.
The alloy contains a high density of lattice distortions.
Lattice distortion induces chemical short-range order and variations in stacking-fault energy.
Above approximately 0.5 Tm, the alloy's yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate.
Elevated-temperature rate-insensitivity is caused by suppression of thermally activated screw-dislocation cross-slip.
The dominant deformation mode shifts from dislocation glide to phase-transformation-assisted slip at elevated temperature.
At low temperature, thermally activated screw-dislocation motion and cross-slip govern deformation and produce strain-rate sensitivity.
At elevated temperature, the energy barrier for cross-slip is overcome.
Short-range order reduces the rate of double-kink nucleation by screw dislocations.
Reduced stacking-fault energy promotes tensile formation of HCP nano-lamellae.
HCP nano-lamellae act as barriers to dislocation motion or facilitate slip.
Phase-transformation kinetics become rate-limiting and thereby decouple yield stress from strain rate.
HCP phase signatures emerge at the yield point when the elevated-temperature rate-insensitive regime is reached.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi ordinarily forms a chemically disordered FCC solid solution below its solidus.
In conventional FCC alloys such as CoCrFeMnNi, yield strength increases monotonically with strain rate across all temperatures because of dislocation drag.
CoCrFeMnNi has no significant phase-transformation contribution at yield.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase FCC HEAs with moderate or low stacking-fault energy and may fail at extremely high stacking-fault energy.
The mechanism may fail when the HCP phase is thermodynamically unstable at the testing temperature.
The temperature threshold for rate-insensitivity depends on atomic-radius mismatch and the resulting local lattice-distortion energy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the elevated-temperature transition to suppression of screw-dislocation cross-slip, whereas the mechanism states that the cross-slip energy barrier is overcome at elevated temperature.
